title: Rabban Yochanan praises his students
hookLine: praising others is part of guarding speech

cards: A teacher sits with his students and describes them, one by one. Of the first he says: a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. Of another: happy is the one who gave birth to him.
Of another: a man of piety. Another: one who fears sin. And of the last: a spring that keeps on flowing, getting stronger as it goes.
The teacher is Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and the scene is in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers. A report card with no grades on it. Only praise, each piece cut to fit one person.

teach.h: HE USED TO RECOUNT THEIR PRAISE.
teach.b: Speak good. Turn it four ways. First, the habit.
Avot doesn't say he praised them once.

teach.h: A CISTERN, A SPRING: PRAISE THAT SEES.
teach.b: It says he used to recount their praise: praise as a practice, done on purpose. After days of what the tongue shouldn't do, here's what it should. Guarding speech isn't only a wall; it's also a road.
Second, the shape of good praise. No two students get the same line. The cistern is for a student who remembered everything he learned.
The spring is for a student whose ideas kept coming.

teach.h: PRAISE THE ONE WHO ISN'T THERE.
teach.b: That's praise that has actually looked at someone. "Great job" is kind. "You never lose a drop" is seen.
Third, a caution, because the tradition is careful even here.
The Talmud warns that praising someone at length can backfire: talk long enough about someone's good side and somebody will start listing the other side.
Maimonides adds that praising a person in front of people who dislike them is a shadow of lashon hara, because it invites the attack.
So speaking good has judgment in it: honest, specific, and said where it builds rather than provokes. Fourth, the absent. Gossip is talk about someone who isn't in the room.

Praise can be too. Saying something good about a person who will never hear it isn't flattery, since there's nothing to gain. It puts their good name back into circulation, the opposite of a cut-open pillow.

how: Jews study Pirkei Avot, including Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's praise of his students; teachers of speech present honest praise of others as part of guarding the tongue, with care not to praise in a way that provokes criticism.

o: flattery that helps you win people's favor
praying aloud with only cheerful words
honest, specific praise, said with judgment

s: guarding speech only means staying quiet
Avot shows a teacher who made praise a habit: speech has a job, not just a wall.
Rabban Yochanan gave each student the same praise
each got his own image: a cistern, a spring, piety, fear of sin.
the tradition warns that praise can backfire
praising at length, or before people who dislike someone, can invite criticism of them.

games.q: you're with colleagues who can't stand a coworker, and you think she did excellent work this week. what do you do?
o: praise her at length right now.
save the praise for a place where it builds her up.
games.why: Maimonides calls praise in front of someone's detractors a shadow of lashon hara: it invites the attack. speak good, with judgment.

practice: Choose a person who won't be in the room with you today, a coworker, a sibling, a teacher from long ago, and look at them the way Rabban Yochanan looked at his students.
Find what is true and particular, not nice or great but an image: the one who always remembers, the one whose kindness keeps flowing.
Shape it into one honest sentence you could say about them; if you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Speak good. In Jewish teaching, guarding speech includes honest, specific praise of others, said with judgment, as Rabban Yochanan praised his students. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: guarding speech includes speaking good. A good name, said aloud, travels too. Speak well, sleep well.
